list.listitem: Do not order serum liver chemistries to screen asymptomatic patients. C

Based on the American College of Gastroenterology guideline (2017), one should repeat the lab panel and/or perform a clarifying test (e.g., gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase [GGT] if serum alkaline phosphate is elevated) to confirm that the liver chemistry is actually abnormal before initiation of evaluation of abnormal liver chemistries. C
Once abnormalities are detected, abnormal liver function tests should be investigated using an individualized approach; see specific algorithms in and . C

The American College of Radiology (ACR, 2023) recommends imaging usually beginning with ultrasound (US) abdomen or US duplex Doppler abdomen, as detailed below, based on the pattern of elevated liver function tests. C

background.definition: Liver function tests (AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase, and bilirubin) are considered abnormal when they fall outside of the normal range (usually 3-5 times above upper limit of normal).The normal range for laboratory values is 2 standard deviations above and below the mean for a reference population. Actual numbers vary based on laboratory equipment and reference population selected.

list.listitem: In a population study in Iceland of patients registered in prescription databases for outpatients and inpatients, the crude annual incidence rate of drug-induced liver injury was 19.1/100,000 (95% CI, 15.4-23.3). Drug-induced injury was defined as an ALT level more than 3-fold the upper limit of normal and/or alkaline phosphatase level more than 2-fold the upper limit of normal.
The prevalence of elevated transaminase levels is estimated at 10%, although less than 5% of these patients have a serious liver disease.

In a British study of 216 children attending a hospital obesity clinic, elevated ALT was identified in 16% with a greater prevalence in boys (23% vs. 10%) and in those with a parental history of type 2 diabetes mellitus (30% vs. 13.2%).
In an audit of primary care practice, physicians failed to investigate 58% of abnormal liver function tests adequately.
Etiologies vary based on which test is abnormal. See for causes of elevated AST/ALT. See for causes of elevated bilirubin. See for causes of elevated alkaline phosphatase.

In the prescription database study in Iceland, the most common drugs causing drug-induced liver injury were amoxicillin-clavulanate (22% of cases), diclofenac (6%), azathioprine (4%), infliximab (4%), and nitrofurantoin (4%). The median duration of therapy was 20 days.

In a review of 5 studies of liver effects following antineoplastic treatment for childhood cancer, the prevalence of hepatic late adverse effects (defined as ALT above the upper limit of normal) ranged from 8.0% to 52.8%, with follow-up durations varying from 1 to 27 years after the end of treatment.

Liver function abnormalities that are mild to moderate and mainly cholestatic are frequently seen in patients with COVID-19. Authors of a retrospective cohort study found that liver patterns showing hepatocellular injury, however, were associated with adverse clinical outcome (odds ratio 3.4, CI 1.7-7). Patients with COVID-19 or influenza whose liver functions did not improve or worsened after 48 hours had a significantly higher risk of death or need for ventilation
ALT and AST levels rise following hepatocellular damage.
Unconjugated bilirubin rises with increased heme breakdown or impaired bilirubin conjugation.
Conjugated bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase rise with intrahepatic cholestasis or extrahepatic biliary obstruction.
Decreased synthetic function of the liver leads to abnormalities of albumin and prothrombin time.

The abnormalities in LFTs in patients with obesity are often attributed to non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), but can also be related to obesity itself due to oxidative stress, insulin resistance, and chronic inflammatory state.

The United States Preventive Services Task Force does not specifically address the use of serum liver chemistries (AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase, and bilirubin) to screen asymptomatic adults for liver disease. C
AST, ALT, and GGT are poor screening tests for excessive alcohol use, fatty liver, and viral hepatitis due to low sensitivities (30%-40%). C

The American Gastroenterological Association (2002), Canadian Medical Association (2005), and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (2006) recommend testing patients with mild elevations of liver enzymes (defined as less than five times the upper limit of normal but above the normal reference range) for hepatitis B and hepatitis C. This approach is hoped to allow earlier diagnosis resulting in better treatment response and decreased progression to cirrhosis.

Differential.Differential_Features: Long-standing alcohol abuse, AST/ALT ratio greater than 2.0
IV drug use, history of blood transfusions, history of travel, pregnancy, AST/ALT ratio less than 1.0, positive serologies
Obesity, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, AST/ALT ratio less than 1.0, no alcohol history
Polypharmacy, illicit drug use, herbal supplement use , idiosyncratic drug reactions
Intestinal bloating, oily stools, positive antigliadin and antiendomysial antibodies
Low thyroid-stimulating hormone, elevated free T4 and T3
Increase in polyclonal immunoglobulins on serum protein electrophoresis
Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, exaggerated by fasting or rifampin
Ductal dilatation on RUQ ultrasound, endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography/magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (ERCP/MRCP) positive for gallstones
Elevated lactase dehydrogenase, decreased haptoglobin, abnormal peripheral blood smear

list.listitem: Most patients with abnormal liver function tests are asymptomatic; abnormalities are found incidentally.
Focus the history on risk factors for liver disease: alcohol use, sexual history, drug abuse, transfusions, and gallbladder disease. A detailed medication history should also be taken (see ).

Focus the physical examination on signs of chronic liver disease or hepatic decompensation: hepatomegaly, ascites, edema, palmar erythema, telangiectasias, jaundice, and scleral icterus. Individual physical signs with the highest likelihood ratios for ruling in cirrhosis are distended abdominal veins (LR+ 15.5), Terry nails (white appearing nail with characteristic "ground glass" appearance and no lunula) (LR+ 14.33), decreased body hair (LR+ 12), and gynecomastia (LR+ 10). Patients with abnormal physical examination need expedited evaluation.
In the Iceland study of drug-induced liver injury, of the 96 patients identified, 26 patients had jaundice and 22 patients were hospitalized.

The body mass index (BMI) should be calculated as part of the physical examination. For severely obese patients (BMI >35), the hypertension and insulin resistance (HAIR) score can be used to calculate the likelihood of nonalcoholic steatohepatitis.
See , and for relevant algorithms.

Liver function tests that show a hepatocellular predominance (elevations in AST and ALT disproportion to elevations in alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin) can be seen in alcoholic and nonalcoholic liver disease, acute hepatitis, and acute liver injury due to other causes. Liver function tests that show a cholestatic pattern (disproportionate elevation in alkaline phosphatase relative to AST and ALT) with or without elevations in GGT and bilirubin can be seen with various causes of biliary obstruction.
In general, AST, ALT, and GGT are poor predictors of hepatitis C, hepatitis B, pancreatitis, and alcohol abuse disorder.

The Canadian Medical Association 2011 guideline on abnormal liver chemistry suggests obtaining an ALT and alkaline phosphatase in patients with suspected liver disease, as elevation of the former can indicate hepatocellular injury while elevation of the latter points to cholestasis as the cause. If the alkaline phosphatase is elevated, an elevated GGT helps to confirm a hepatobiliary origin; if not elevated, bone origin is suspected.

The ACR recommends the following as usually appropriate for initial imaging in cases of abnormal liver function tests:
Hepatocellular predominance with mild aminotransferase increase, recommend US abdomen or US duplex Doppler abdomen. US shear wave elastography, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), or CT abdomen/pelvis without contrast may also be appropriate. Cholestatic predominance recommend US abdomen, MRI abdomen without and with contrast plus magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography MRCP, or CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast. Hyperbilirubinemia (acute or subacute cholestasis) recommend US abdomen, MRI abdomen without and with contrast plus MRCP, MRI abdomen without contrast plus MRCP, or CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast.
For elevation of ALT/AST, see algorithm in .
For elevation of bilirubin, see algorithm in .
For elevation of alkaline phosphatase, see algorithm in .

ACG guidelines recommend that an initial evaluation for a patient with elevated ALT or AST <5x upper limit of normal begin with a history and physical including assessment for metabolic syndrome and insulin resistance, discontinuation of hepatotoxic medications, cessation of alcohol consumption, and evaluation for risk factors for hepatosteatosis and hepatitis B or C. Initial blood tests should include tests for hepatitis B and C, an iron panel, lipid panel, complete blood count with platelets, blood glucose or hemoglobin A1c and abdominal ultrasound. If that fails to confirm the diagnosis, consider either observation or additional blood tests including ANA, anti-smooth muscle antibodies, ceruloplasmin to assess for Wilson's disease, TSH, tests for celiac disease, and alpha-1 antitrypsin.

For patients with moderate (5-15 ULN) elevation, an initial evaluation including all of the above test is recommended, with consultation with a hepatologist in most cases. For patients with severe elevations above 15 x ULN, also obtain a serum drug panel, urine toxicology, and consider n-acetyl cysteine urgently if possible acetaminophen ingestion.

Use the NAFLD Fibrosis Score (nafldscore.com) to assess the likelihood of fibrosis in patients with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. Patients with a score >0.675 are at high risk of advanced fibrosis and should be referred to a hepatologist. Those with a score <-1.455 are at low risk for fibrosis and should be managed with weight loss and management of cardiovascular risk factors. Those with an intermediate score (-1.455-0.675) should undergo elastography (FibroScan) or a serum enhanced liver fibrosis test.

algorithm.title: Mild Elevations of Serum ALT and AST: Diagnosis.

cell.label: Elevated ALT and AST less than 5 times normal
History and physical examination. Discontinue hepatotoxic medications and alcohol.
Consider repeat ALT/AST or a clarifying test to confirm abnormality.
Liver chemistries, PT, albumin, CBC with platelets, Hepatitis A, B, and C serologies, serum iron, total iron binding capacity, ferritin, glucose or hemoglobin A1C, and abdominal ultrasound.
Proceed with directed evaluation and treatment.
Symptomatic or evidence of hepatic decompensation?
Expedited evaluation.
Lifestyle modification: Discontinue alcohol. Stop hepatotoxic medications. Weight loss. Diabetes control.
Six-month follow-up: Repeat liver chemistries.
Observation.
Elastography and labs: ANA, anti-smooth muscle antibody, ceruloplasmin, alpha1-antitrypsin, antigliadin, antiendomysial antibody.

feature.caption: Etiology of ALT or AST Elevations.
feature.feature_body:
Mild elevation (<5 times upper limit of normal)
Common hepatic causes
• Alcohol
• Chronic hepatitis B
• Chronic hepatitis C
• Acute viral hepatitis (hepatitis A-E, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus)
• Steatosis/steatohepatitis
Medications/toxins
Uncommon hepatic causes
• Hemochromatosis
• Autoimmune hepatitis
• Alpha1-antitrypsin deficiency
• Wilson's disease
Nonhepatic causes
• Celiac disease
• Hemolysis
• Strenuous exercise
• Muscle disease
• Thyroid disease
Severe elevation (≥5 times upper limit of normal)
Acute viral hepatitis
Ischemic hepatitis/hypotension
Medications/toxins
Acute bile duct obstruction (ie, gallstones)
Acute Budd-Chiari syndrome
Autoimmune hepatitis
Wilson's disease
